# In Praise of the Blank Space

There is a persistent myth that medieval mapmakers wrote "here be dragons" on the edges of the known world. In reality, almost no historical map says this. The phrase appears, in Latin, on just one surviving globe, the Hunt-Lenox Globe from around 1510. Yet the idea has lodged itself so firmly in our imagination that we assume it must be true. I think this says something about us. We want the edges of maps to be populated with menace and wonder, because the alternative, an honest blank, is harder to sit with.

I've been thinking about blank spaces lately, and about how rarely we allow them.

Consider what a map does. It is an argument that the world can be reduced to something you can hold in your hands. A good map lies constantly and usefully. It flattens a sphere, erases most of what exists, and picks a few features to elevate: roads, rivers, borders. The London Underground map is the famous example. It abandons geography entirely in favor of topology, and it is better for it, because what a traveler needs is not distance but connection. Every map is a decision about what to leave out.

The blank space is the one place where a map admits the decision was forced on it. Ignorance shows there in its plainest form. The old cartographers who left the interior of Africa empty, or drew a coastline as a tentative dotted line, were doing something more intellectually honest than the ones who filled the gaps with invented mountain ranges. There was a real one of those, the Mountains of Kong, a fictional range that appeared on European maps for nearly a century, copied from map to map because each cartographer trusted the last. Nobody had invented it maliciously. It was a plausible guess that hardened into fact through repetition. The blank would have been more truthful.

This happens everywhere, not just in geography. Most of us carry around internal maps of subjects we have never really examined: how the economy works, what our neighbors think, why a friendship cooled. We fill in these regions with confident-looking mountains. The feeling of understanding is cheap to produce, and a blank feels like failure, so we draw something. Psychologists call one version of this the illusion of explanatory depth. Ask people whether they understand how a zipper or a toilet works and they say yes. Ask them to explain it step by step and they discover, often with visible surprise, that the region they thought was charted is empty.

I find that moment of discovery oddly pleasant. There is a small vertigo in it, then a kind of relief. The map was wrong, and now I know where. A known blank is an asset, since it tells you where to go next. An unknown blank, a place you believe is filled but isn't, is a hazard.

So the skill worth cultivating is not simply knowing more, though that helps. It is knowing the borders of what you know, and being able to feel them. Some people seem to have this naturally. You ask them a question and they say, "I know about this part, but past here I'm guessing." The best doctors I've encountered talk this way, and so do the best teachers and the best mechanics. Their confidence is not a uniform coat of paint. It has texture: firm here, soft there, absent over there. Talking with them is like reading a map that includes its own margin of error.

The opposite type is exhausting. Their confidence is flat and total, and the same tone of voice covers what they know cold and what they read in a headline that morning. You can't navigate by them, because there is no signal in the noise. Everything is a mountain.

Blank spaces matter beyond knowledge, too. Think of a calendar. A week with every hour scheduled is a map with no unexplored territory, and it has a claustrophobic quality even when every entry is something you want to do. The unscheduled afternoon is where odd things happen: a walk that goes somewhere unplanned, a thought that needs forty minutes of idleness before it will show itself. Boredom, which we now treat as a malfunction to be fixed instantly with a phone, may be the mind's way of surveying its own blank regions. Take away the emptiness and you take away the place where new things can be drawn.

Or think of conversation. A good conversation has silences in it, gaps where neither person rushes to fill the air. Anxious talkers cover every pause, and the result is a kind of noise that feels social but leaves nothing behind. The pause is where the other person gets room to say the true thing, the one that takes a moment to assemble. A conversation with no blanks is a conversation with no unexplored territory, and so nothing can be found.

I don't want to romanticize ignorance. Blank spaces on real maps eventually got filled by people who went out and measured, often at great cost, and the filling-in was mostly a good thing. Curiosity is not the same as contentment with not knowing. The point is to be honest about the state of the map, so that when we go exploring we know we are exploring, and when we're guessing we know we're guessing. The mistake is not having blanks. The mistake is painting over them.

There's a small practice I've found useful. When I notice I'm holding a strong opinion, I try to ask what the territory underneath it looks like. Have I walked it, or just seen it on someone else's map? Often the answer is humbling, but it's also freeing. I get to put down the burden of pretending, and I get an errand: go and look.

The dragons, it turns out, were never on the old maps. We added them later, because we couldn't bear the plain white paper. But the plain white paper was doing something braver. It said: nobody knows what's here yet. Come and see.

I think I'd like to live more like that, with a map that has honest edges, some dotted coastlines, and a few wide, clean stretches of nothing, kept open on purpose.
